annotations.title: Vnderſtanding.
annotations.text: VVhen Dauid had ſinned and ſomewhile neglected to confeſſe his fault, [1]Gods mercie by affliction made him to vnderſtand his owne eſtate, who then repenting, confeſſing, and ſorowing for his ſinnes made this Pſalme. which is therfore intitled Vnderſtanding: or, Inſtruction of Dauid. [2]It geueth vs alſo to vnderſtand, and to know, ſaith S. Auguſtin, that we muſt neither truſt in our owne merites, nor preſume to eſcape puniſhment of ſinne. Thy firſt vnderſtanding therfore or leſſon, muſt be, to know thy ſelf to be a ſinner. The next is, [3]that when with faith thou beginneſt to worke wel by loue, thou attribute not this to thyn owne ſtreingth, but to the grace of God.

annotations.title: VVhoſe ſins are couered. 2. not imputed.
annotations.text: Caluin and his complices gather poyſon of theſe holie words [1] [2], denying that ſins are truly taken away, but only couered, and ſtil remayne ſay they in the iuſteſt. Which ſenſe would make this Scripture contrarie to other places. Iſaie 6. Thyn iniquitie shal be taken away, and thy ſinne ſhal be cleanſed. Ioan. 1. The lambe of God which taketh away the ſins of the world. Act. 3. Be penitent & conuert, that your ſins may be put out. 1. Cor. 6. You are washed, you are ſanctified, you are iuſtified: & the like, which shew the true real taking away of ſins, true ſanctification and iuſtification. As S. Jerome (or ſome other ancient authentical Author) explicateth this place ſaying: Sins are ſo couered by baptiſm & penance [3], that they are not to be revealed in the day of iudgement, nor imputed in him that diligently purgeth himſelf in this world, or by martyrdom. S. Auguſtine teacheth the ſame, ſaying: Sins are couered, are wholly couered, are aboliſhed. Neither muſt you vnderſtand (ſaith he) that ſins are couered, as though ſtil they were, & liued. VVhy then did the Prophet ſay: ſins are couered? They are not to be puniſhed. More clearly li. 1. c. 13. cont. duas Epiſt. Pelag. The Pelagians calumniating Catholics, as if they taught, that ſins are not taken away, but ſhauen, as hairs are cut with a razor; the roots remaining in the fleſh: which (he anſwereth) none affirmeth but an infidel Likewiſe S. Gregorie teacheth, that a ſinner couereth his ſins wel when with contrarie virtues he ouerwhelmeth former vices, and with good deeds blotteth out former euil deeds. He couereth them euil, when either for ſhame, or feare, or obſtinacie, or deſperation, he concealeth his ſins, omitting to confeſſe them. God couereth ſins [4], as a phyſician couereth wounds, by applying medicinal plaſter, which indeed cureth them. Thus ancient learned holie Fathers expound this text. Further explicating, that albeit things couered, and only thereby hidde from men, do remaine as they were before they were hid, yet whatſoeuer is hid to God, is indeed vtterly taken away, for nothing that is, can be hid from God. And the contrarie doctrin of Proteſtants is injurious either to God's power [5], if they ſay he cannot quite take away ſins; or to his mercie, if he will not; or to his iuſtice, if he neuer puniſh ſins euer remayning; and to his truth, if he repute otherwiſe, than indeed the thing is. It is alſo injurious to Chriſt [6], to ſay, his blood and death is not effectual to take away ſins: injurious to innumerable places of holie Scripture [7], which affirme plainly that ſins by God's grace are vtterly taken away: Finally, it is injurious to Saints in heauen [8], arguing them as ſtil infected with ſins, if indeed ſins yet remaine in them: which is moſt abſurde, and blaſphemie to ſpeake. And yet foloweth by neceſſarie conſequence. For if the iuſteſt liued & died in ſinne, they ſhould remaine eternally in ſinne.

notes.text: Protestants expound this place contrary to many other clear places.
Contrary to the exposition of ancient fathers.
God covering or not imputing sins doth quite take them away.
The contrary doctrine is injurious to God:

annotations.title: Neither is there guile in his ſpirite.
annotations.text: In remiſſion of ſinnes the penitent neceſſarily muſt ſo cooperate, <mn>[1]</mn>that he haue no guile in his ſpirite, or hart, for if he haue, then he faileth of the forſaide bleſſednes, and his iniquities are not forgeuen, nor his ſinnes couered to God, but to be imputed and puniſhed. Yet the repentance of a ſinner be it neuer ſo ſincere, hartie, and without guile doth not merite remiſſion of ſinne, but only diſpoſeth therto. But after remiſſion it is ſatisfactorie for the paine due for ſinnes, <mn>[2]</mn>and meritorious of glorie. According as S. Auguſtin here teacheth ſaying Good (or meritorious) workes goe not before faith, and remiſſion, but folow the ſame.

notes.text: Sincere repentance is a necessarie dispotion to remission of sinne.
After remission it is satisfactorie and meritorious.
